questions.prompt: How do you remove a single point of failure?

options.text: Add redundancy — run more than one so losing one is survivable

questions.explanation: A SPOF is removed by redundancy: running spare capacity (N+1, active-active or active-passive) so the failure of one instance doesn't take down the system.

questions.prompt: Why must redundant copies be placed in different failure domains?

options.text: Because redundancy only helps if the copies don't fail together; copies in one rack/zone can all die at once
It doesn't matter where they are

questions.explanation: Three replicas in one rack all fail if that rack loses power. Spreading across zones/regions makes failures independent, which is the point of redundancy.

questions.prompt: Why is replication NOT a substitute for backups?

options.text: Replication faithfully propagates corruption and accidental deletes to all replicas instantly; backups are point-in-time copies you can restore from

questions.explanation: If a bug or bad DELETE corrupts data, replication copies the damage everywhere. A backup is a point-in-time copy that lets you recover — so you need both.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Maximum acceptable time to restore service
Maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time
A standby takes over on failure

questions.explanation: RTO is downtime tolerance, RPO is data-loss tolerance; active-active runs all units live, active-passive keeps a standby ready.

questions.prompt: A team runs three database replicas in the same rack 'for low latency.' What's the flaw?

options.text: They share a failure domain, so a rack power loss kills all three at once
Replicas can't be in the same rack technically

questions.explanation: Co-locating replicas in one failure domain means one rack outage takes them all down, defeating the purpose of redundancy. Spread them across zones.

options.text: Deliberately injecting failures in a controlled way to verify redundancy and failover actually work

questions.explanation: Chaos engineering intentionally introduces failures (killing instances, adding latency, simulating outages) under controlled conditions to prove the system's resilience before a real outage does.
